The von Mises transformation: order reduction and construction of Bäcklund transformations and new integrable equations

Andrei D. Polyanin Note: Institute for Problems in Mechanics, Russian Academy of Sciences, 101 Vernadsky Avenue, bldg 1, 119526 Moscow, Russia. E-mail: polyanin@ipmnet.ru    Alexei I. Zhurov Note: Institute for Problems in Mechanics, Russian Academy of Sciences, 101 Vernadsky Avenue, bldg 1, 119526 Moscow, Russia; School of Dentistry, Cardiff University, Heath Park, Cardiff CF14 4XY, UK. E-mail: zhurovai@cardiff.ac.uk
Original version 3 July 2009, revised 17 July 2009
Abstract

Wide classes of nonlinear mathematical physics equations are described that admit order reduction through the use of the von Mises transformation, with the unknown function taken as the new independent variable and an appropriate partial derivative taken as the new dependent variable. RF-pairs and associated Bäcklund transformations are constructed for evolution equations of general form (special cases of which are Burgers, Korteweg–de Vries, and Harry Dym type equations as well as many other nonlinear equations of mathematical physics). The results obtained are used for order reduction and constructing exact solutions of hydrodynamics equations. A generalized Calogero equation and a number of other new integrable nonlinear equations are considered.

Keywords: nonlinear partial differential equations; mathematical physics; von Mises transformation; Bäcklund transformations; RF-pairs; integrable equations; order reduction; exact solutions; generalized Calogero equation; hydrodynamics equations

1 Preliminary remarks

A simple analogue of the von Mises transformation is widely used in the theory of ordinary differential equations. Specifically, an nnth-order autonomous ordinary differential equation of general form,

F⁡(u,ux′,ux​x′′,…,ux(n))=0,F(u,u^{\prime}_{x},u^{\prime\prime}_{xx},\dots,u^{(n)}_{x})=0, (1)

which does not depend explicitly on xx, can be reduced with the change of variable

η⁡(u)=ux′(analogue of the von Mises transformation)\eta(u)=u^{\prime}_{x}\qquad(\mbox{\it analogue of the von Mises transformation}) (2)

to an (n−1)(n-1)st-order equation (e.g., see [1, 2]).

For partial differential equations, the von Mises transformation (with the unknown function and its appropriate partial derivative taken as the new independent and dependent variables, respectively) is applied for order reduction of steady hydrodynamic boundary layer equations [3–5].

An RF-pair is an operation of consecutive raising and lowering of the order of an equation (RF stands for “Rise” and “Fall”). To illustrate this concept, let us solve the nnth-order ordinary differential equation of general form

F⁡(x,u,ux′,ux​x′′,…,ux(n))=0F(x,u,u^{\prime}_{x},u^{\prime\prime}_{xx},\dots,u^{(n)}_{x})=0 (3)

for the independent variable (which is assumed to be feasible) to obtain

G⁡(u,ux′,ux​x′′,…,ux(n))=x.G(u,u^{\prime}_{x},u^{\prime\prime}_{xx},\dots,u^{(n)}_{x})=x. (4)

Differentiating (4) with respect to xx yields an (n+1)(n+1)st-order autonomous equation, whose order is further reduced using substitution (2). As a result, we arrive at the nnth-order equation

η​dd​u​G​(u,η,η​ηu′,…,ηx(n−1))=1.\eta\frac{d}{du}G(u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u}^{\prime},\dots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{x})=1. (5)

The derivatives with respect to xx are found consecutively using ηx(k)=η​(ηx(k−1))u\eta^{(k)}_{x}=\eta(\eta^{(k-1)}_{x})_{u}. The derivative with respect to uu on the left-hand side of (5) is calculated by the chain rule taking into account that FF depends on uu, η\eta, ηu\eta_{u}, …

Equations (4) and (5) are related by the Bäcklund transformation

G⁡(u,η,ηx′,…,ηx(n−1))=x,ux′=η.\begin{array}[]{rcl}G(u,\eta,\eta^{\prime}_{x},\dots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{x})&=&x,\\ u^{\prime}_{x}&=&\eta.\end{array} (6)

Many new integrable ordinary differential equations have been found in a systematic manner using RF-pair operations and associated Bäcklund transformations [2, 6].

The above ideas and results for ordinary differential equations turn out to be transferrable, when appropriately modified, to nonlinear partial differential equations. The present paper will describe wide classes of nonlinear mathematical physics equations that admit order reduction with the Mises transformation. This transformation will then be used to construct RF-pairs and Bäcklund transformations for nonlinear evolution equations of general form. This will result in finding new integrable nonlinear equations.

Various Bäcklund transformations and their applications to specific mathematical physics equations can be found, for example, in [5, 7–17].

In the present paper, the term integrable equation applies to nonlinear partial differential equations that admit solution in terms of quadratures or can be linearized (i.e., their solutions can be expressed in terms of solutions to linear differential equations or linear integral equations).

2 Using the von Mises transformation for order
reduction of partial differential equations

Consider the nonlinear nnth-order equation [5, p. 678]

∂u∂x​∂2u∂t​∂x−∂u∂t​∂2u∂x2=F⁡(t,u,∂u∂x,∂2u∂x2,…,∂nu∂xn).\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial t\mkern 1.0mu\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}=F\left(t,u,\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}},\ldots,\frac{\partial^{n}u}{\partial x^{n}}\right). (7)

In the special case F=ν​ux​x​xF=\nu u_{xxx}, this is a nonlinear third-order equation that describes a laminar boundary layer of a non-Newtonian fluid on a flat plate, with uu being the stream function, tt and xx spatial coordinates measured along and across the plate, and ν\nu the kinematic fluid viscosity [3–5].

1∘. Characteristic property of Eq. (7). Let u~​(t,x)\widetilde{u}(t,x) be a solution to the above equation. Then the function

u⁡(t,x)=u~​(t,x+φ⁡(t)),u(t,x)=\widetilde{u}\left(t,\,x+\varphi(t)\right),

with an arbitrary function φ⁡(t)\varphi(t), is also a solution to the equation.

2∘. In Eq. (7), let us pass from the old variables to the Mises variables:

t,x,u=u⁡(t,x)⟹t,u,η=η⁡(t,u),whereη=∂u∂x.t,\ x,\ u=u(t,x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t,\ u,\ \eta=\eta(t,u),\ \ \hbox{where}\ \ \eta=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}. (8)

The derivatives are transformed as follows:

∂∂x=∂u∂x​∂∂u=η​∂∂u,∂∂t=∂∂t+∂u∂t​∂∂u,\frac{\partial}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}=\eta\frac{\partial}{\partial u},\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}, (9)
∂2u∂x2=η∂η∂u,∂3u∂x3=η∂∂u(η∂η∂u),…;∂2u∂t​∂x=∂η∂t+∂u∂t∂η∂u.\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}=\eta\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u},\quad\frac{\partial^{3}u}{\partial x^{3}}=\eta\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\eta\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u}\right),\quad\dots;\quad\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial t\mkern 1.0mu\partial x}=\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u}. (10)

As a result, the von Mises transformation (8) reduces the nnth-order equation (7) to the (n−1)(n-1)st-order equation

η​∂η∂t=F⁡(t,u,η,η​∂η∂u,…,∂n−1η∂xn−1),\eta\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}=F\left(t,u,\eta,\eta\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u},\ldots,\frac{\partial^{n-1}\eta}{\partial x^{n-1}}\right), (11)

where the higher derivatives are calculated as

∂ku∂xk=∂k−1η∂xk−1=η∂∂u∂k−2η∂xk−2,∂∂x=η∂∂u,k=3,…,n.\frac{\partial^{k}u}{\partial x^{k}}=\frac{\partial^{k-1}\eta}{\partial x^{k-1}}=\eta\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\frac{\partial^{k-2}\eta}{\partial x^{k-2}},\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial x}=\eta\frac{\partial}{\partial u},\quad k=3,\dots,n.

Short notation for partial derivatives (e.g., uxu_{x}, ux​xu_{xx}, ux​tu_{xt}, etc.) will sometimes be used in what follows.

Example 1. Equation (7) with F=f⁡(t,u)​ux​x+g⁡(t,u)​ux2+h⁡(t,u)​ux=f⁡(t,u)​η​ηu+g⁡(t,u)​η2+h⁡(t,u)​ηF=f(t,u)u_{xx}+g(t,u)u_{x}^{2}+h(t,u)u_{x}=f(t,u)\eta\eta_{u}+g(t,u)\eta^{2}+h(t,u)\eta is reduced to an equation (11) of a special form, which is further reduced, after canceling by η\eta, to a linear first-order equation:

ηt−f⁡(t,u)​ηu=g⁡(t,u)​η+h⁡(t,u).\eta_{t}-f(t,u)\eta_{u}=g(t,u)\eta+h(t,u).

Example 2. If F=f⁡(t,u)​ux​x​x/ux=f⁡(t,u)​(η​ηu)uF=f(t,u)u_{xxx}/u_{x}=f(t,u)(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}, Eq. (11) is reduced with the change of variable Z=η2Z=\eta^{2} to a linear second-order equation: Zt=f⁡(t,u)​Zu​uZ_{t}=f(t,u)Z_{uu}.

Given below are two possible generalizations of Eq. (7).

1∘. Equation (7) can be generalized by including IxI_{x}, …, Ix(m)I_{x}^{(m)}, where I=ux​ut​x−ut​ux​xI=u_{x}u_{tx}-u_{t}u_{xx}, into FF as additional arguments.

2∘. The von Mises transformation (8) reduces the order of the equation

ux​Gt−ut​Gx=F⁡(t,u,ux,…,ux(n)),G=G⁡(t,u,ux,…,ux(m)),u_{x}G_{t}-u_{t}G_{x}=F(t,u,u_{x},\ldots,u_{x}^{(n)}),\quad G=G(t,u,u_{x},\ldots,u_{x}^{(m)}), (12)

and brings it to the form (11), where ηt\eta_{t} must be replaced with GtG_{t}. If G=uxG=u_{x}, Eq. (12) coincides with Eq. (7).

Example 3. The nonlinear third-order equation

ux​ut​x​x−ut​ux​x​x=f⁡(t,u)​uxu_{x}u_{txx}-u_{t}u_{xxx}=f(t,u)u_{x} (13)

is a special case of Eq. (12) with G=ux​xG=u_{xx} and F=f⁡(t,u)​uxF=f(t,u)u_{x}. The von Mises transformation (8) brings it to the second-order equation (η​ηu)t=f⁡(t,u)(\eta\eta_{u})_{t}=f(t,u), whose general solution is given by

η2=2​∫t0t∫u0uf⁡(τ,ξ)​𝑑ξ​𝑑τ+φ⁡(t)+ψ⁡(u),\eta^{2}=2\int^{t}_{t_{0}}\!\!\int^{u}_{u_{0}}f(\tau,\xi)\,d\xi\,d\tau+\varphi(t)+\psi(u),

where φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) and ψ⁡(u)\psi(u) arbitrary functions and t0t_{0} and u0u_{0} are arbitrary constants.

Remark. Other partial differential equations that admit order reduction will be considered below in Section 6.

3 Using the von Mises transformation for constructing RF-pairs and Bäcklund transformations

Consider the nnth-order evolution equation of general form

ut=s⁡(t)​x​ux+F⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,…,ux(n)).u_{t}=s(t)xu_{x}+F(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},\dots,u^{(n)}_{x}). (14)

The Burgers, Korteweg–de Vries, and Harry Dym equations as well as many other nonlinear mathematical physics equations [5, 7–9] are special cases of Eq. (14).

1∘. Characteristic property of Eq. (14). Let u~​(t,x)\widetilde{u}(t,x) be a solution to the above equation. Then the function

u=u~(t,x+ψ(t)),ψ(t)=Cexp(−∫s(t)dt),u=\widetilde{u}(t,\,x+\psi(t)),\quad\psi(t)=C\exp\left(-\int s(t)\,dt\right),

where CC is an arbitrary constant, is also a solution to this equation.

2∘. Suitable RF-pair operations are performed using the formula

∂∂x​(utux)≡ux​ut​x−ut​ux​xux2=ηtη.\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{u_{t}}{u_{x}}\right)\equiv\frac{u_{x}u_{tx}-u_{t}u_{xx}}{u_{x}^{2}}=\frac{\eta_{t}}{\eta}. (15)

It is obtained by differentiating the ratio of the derivatives ut/uxu_{t}/u_{x} with respect to xx followed by passing from tt, xx, uu to the von Mises variables (8).

Let us divide both sides of Eq. (14) by uxu_{x} and differentiate with respect to xx. The left-hand side of the resulting (n+1)(n+1)st-order equation coincides with (15). By passing to the von Mises variables (8) and rearranging, we arrive at the nnth-order equation

ηt=s⁡(t)​η+η2​∂∂u​(Fη),F=F⁡(t,u,η,η​ηu,…,ηx(n−1)).\eta_{t}=s(t)\eta+\eta^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\frac{F}{\eta}\right),\quad F=F(t,u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u},\dots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{x}). (16)

The partial derivatives with respect to xx are calculated successively using ηx(k)=η​(ηx(k−1))u\eta^{(k)}_{x}=\eta(\eta^{(k-1)}_{x})_{u}. The derivative with respect to uu on the right-hand side of Eq. (16) is obtained by the chain rule taking into account that FF depends on uu, η\eta, ηu\eta_{u}, …

3∘. Equations (14) and (16) are related by the Bäcklund transformation

ut=s⁡(t)​x​η+F⁡(t,u,η,ηx,…,ηx(n−1)),ux=η.\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&s(t)x\eta+F(t,u,\eta,\eta_{x},\dots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{x}),\\ u_{x}&=&\eta.\end{array} (17)

Any solution u=g⁡(t,x)u=g(t,x) to Eq. (14) determines a solution to Eq. (16), which can be represented in parametric form as u=g⁡(t,x)u=g(t,x), η=gx​(t,x)\eta=g_{x}(t,x).

Suppose η=η⁡(t,u)\eta=\eta(t,u) is a solution to Eq. (16). Then it follows from the second equation in (17) that

∫d​uη⁡(t,u)=x+φ⁡(t),\int\frac{du}{\eta(t,u)}=x+\varphi(t), (18)

where φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) is an arbitrary function. Further, on solving Eq. (18) for u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x), one should substitute the resulting expression into the original equation (14) and determine φ⁡(t)\varphi(t).

Remark. It is sometimes convenient to rewrite Eq. (16) in the form

ζt=−s⁡(t)​ζ−∂∂u​(ζ​F),ζ=1η.\zeta_{t}=-s(t)\zeta-\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\zeta F),\quad\zeta=\frac{1}{\eta}.

4 Using the von Mises transformation for constructing new integrable nonlinear equations

Below are examples of using the Bäcklund transformation (17) to construct new integrable nonlinear equations of mathematical physics.

Example 1. Consider the generalized Burgers equation

ut+f⁡(u)​ux=a​ux​x.u_{t}+f(u)u_{x}=au_{xx}. (19)

The Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=a​ηx−f⁡(u)​η=a​η​ηu−f⁡(u)​ηF=a\eta_{x}-f(u)\eta=a\eta\eta_{u}-f(u)\eta and s⁡(t)≡0s(t)\equiv 0 brings Eq. (19) to the equation ηt=a​η2​ηu​u−fu′​(u)​η2\eta_{t}=a\eta^{2}\eta_{uu}-f^{\prime}_{u}(u)\eta^{2}, which is further reduced with the substitution η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta to the nonlinear heat equation with a source

ζt=a​(ζ−2​ζu)u+fu′​(u).\zeta_{t}=a(\zeta^{-2}\zeta_{u})_{u}+f^{\prime}_{u}(u). (20)

By setting f⁡(u)=b​uf(u)=bu in (19), we arrive at an integrable equation (20) (reducible to the classical Burgers equation (19)), which was derived in [18] (see also [5, 19]) using a different method.

Example 2. Consider the nonlinear second-order equation

ut=ux​x+f⁡(u)​ux2.u_{t}=u_{xx}+f(u)u_{x}^{2}. (21)

It is reducible, with the change of variable [5, p. 87]

w=∫F⁡(u)​𝑑u,F⁡(u)=exp⁡[∫f⁡(u)​𝑑u],w=\int F(u)\,du,\quad\ F(u)=\exp\left[\int f(u)\,du\right],

to the linear heat equation wt=wx​xw_{t}=w_{xx}.

The Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=ηx+f⁡(u)​η2=η​ηu+f⁡(u)​η2F=\eta_{x}+f(u)\eta^{2}=\eta\eta_{u}+f(u)\eta^{2} and s⁡(t)≡0s(t)\equiv 0 reduces Eq. (21) to the new integrable nonlinear equation

ηt=η2​ηu​u+η2​[f⁡(u)​η]u.\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}\eta_{uu}+\eta^{2}[f(u)\eta]_{u}.

Example 3. The linear third-order equation

ut=a​ux​x​x+b​ux​x+s​x​uxu_{t}=au_{xxx}+bu_{xx}+sxu_{x}

with arbitrary functional coefficients a=a⁡(t)a=a(t), b=b⁡(t)b=b(t), and s=s⁡(t)s=s(t) can be reduced, using the Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=a​ηx​x+b​ηx=a​η​(η​ηu)u+b​η​ηuF=a\eta_{xx}+b\eta_{x}=a\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}+b\eta\eta_{u} followed by substituting η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta, to a new integrable equation

ζt+s​ζ=a​(ζ−3​ζu)u​u+b​(ζ−2​ζu)u.\zeta_{t}+s\zeta=a(\zeta^{-3}\zeta_{u})_{uu}+b(\zeta^{-2}\zeta_{u})_{u}. (22)

In the special cases a=s=0a=s=0 and b=s=0b=s=0, we have simpler nonlinear equations, which were studied in [18] and [5, p. 26, 534].

Example 4. Consider the nonlinear third-order equation

ut+f⁡(u)​ux=a​ux​x​x.u_{t}+f(u)u_{x}=au_{xxx}. (23)

If f⁡(u)=constf(u)=\hbox{const}, it is linear. For f⁡(u)=b​uf(u)=bu and f⁡(u)=b​u2f(u)=bu^{2}, it becomes the Korteweg–de Vries and modified Korteweg–de Vries equation [5, 7], respectively. The Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=a​ηx​x−f⁡(u)​η=a​η​(η​ηu)u−f⁡(u)​ηF=a\eta_{xx}-f(u)\eta=a\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}-f(u)\eta and s⁡(t)≡0s(t)\equiv 0 brings Eq. (23) to the equation ηt=a​η2​(η​ηu)u​u−fu′​(u)​η2\eta_{t}=a\eta^{2}(\eta\eta_{u})_{uu}-f^{\prime}_{u}(u)\eta^{2}, which is further reduced with the change of variable η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta to the form

ζt=a​(ζ−3​ζu)u​u+fu′​(u).\zeta_{t}=a(\zeta^{-3}\zeta_{u})_{uu}+f^{\prime}_{u}(u). (24)

The special case of this equation with f⁡(u)≡0f(u)\equiv 0 was obtained in [5, p. 534] by a different method.

Also, setting f⁡(u)=b​uf(u)=bu and f⁡(u)=b​u2f(u)=bu^{2} in (24) gives the integrable equations

ζt\displaystyle\zeta_{t} =\displaystyle= a​(ζ−3​ζu)u​u+b,\displaystyle a(\zeta^{-3}\zeta_{u})_{uu}+b, (25)
ζt\displaystyle\zeta_{t} =\displaystyle= a​(ζ−3​ζu)u​u+2​b​u.\displaystyle a(\zeta^{-3}\zeta_{u})_{uu}+2bu. (26)

Example 5. Consider the third-order equation

ut=a​ux​x​x+b​uxn,u_{t}=au_{xxx}+bu_{x}^{n}, (27)

which is linear for n=0n=0 and n=1n=1 and also integrable for n=2n=2 and n=3n=3 [5, 7]. The Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=a​ux​x​x+b​uxn=a​η​(η​ηu)u+b​ηnF=au_{xxx}+bu_{x}^{n}=a\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}+b\eta^{n} and s⁡(t)≡0s(t)\equiv 0 brings Eq. (27) to a nonlinear equation, which is further reduced with the change of variable η=θ1/2\eta=\theta^{1/2} to the form

θt=a​θ3/2​θu​u​u+b⁡(n−1)​θn/2​θu.\theta_{t}=a\theta^{3/2}\theta_{uuu}+b(n-1)\theta^{n/2}\theta_{u}. (28)

In particular, setting n=2n=2 and n=3n=3 in (28) gives the integrable equations

θt\displaystyle\theta_{t} =\displaystyle= a​θ3/2​θu​u​u+b​θ​θu,\displaystyle a\theta^{3/2}\theta_{uuu}+b\theta\theta_{u},
θt\displaystyle\theta_{t} =\displaystyle= a​θ3/2​θu​u​u+2​b​θ3/2​θu.\displaystyle a\theta^{3/2}\theta_{uuu}+2b\theta^{3/2}\theta_{u}.

Example 6. The nonlinear third-order equation

ut=f⁡(u)​ux​x​xu_{t}=f(u)u_{xxx} (29)

is integrable for f⁡(u)=a​u3/2f(u)=au^{3/2} [5, p. 535] (cf. Eq. (28) with b=0b=0) and f⁡(u)=a​u3f(u)=au^{3} (Harry Dym equation) [5, p. 528]. The Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=f⁡(u)​ηx​x=f⁡(u)​η​(η​ηu)uF=f(u)\eta_{xx}=f(u)\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u} and s⁡(t)≡0s(t)\equiv 0 reduces Eq. (29) to the equation ηt=η2​[f⁡(u)​(η​ηu)u]u\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}[f(u)(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}]_{u}, which can also be rewritten as

θt=θ3/2​[f⁡(u)​θu​u]u,θ=η2.\displaystyle\theta_{t}=\theta^{3/2}[f(u)\theta_{uu}]_{u},\quad\ \theta=\eta^{2}.

Example 7. The linear fourth-order equation ut=a​ux​x​x​xu_{t}=au_{xxxx} can be reduced, using the Bäcklund transformation (17) with F=a​ηx​x​x=a​η​[η​(η​ηu)u]uF=a\eta_{xxx}=a\eta[\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u}]_{u} and s≡0s\equiv 0 followed by the change of variable η=θ1/2\eta=\theta^{1/2}, to the nonlinear fourth-order equation

θt=a​θ3/2​(θ1/2​θu​u)u​u.\theta_{t}=a\theta^{3/2}(\theta^{1/2}\theta_{uu})_{uu}. (30)

Remark. More new integrable equations may be obtained by applying a Bäcklund transformation of the form (17), based on the von Mises transformation, to each of the equations (20) (with f⁡(u)=b​uf(u)=bu), (22), (25), (28), and (30).

5 Using the von Mises transformation for integro-
differential equations

Consider integro-differential equations of the form

ut=F⁡(t,u,ux,ux​x,…,ux(n))+ux​∫x0xG⁡(t,u,uz,uz​z,…,uz(m))​𝑑z.u_{t}=F(t,u,u_{x},u_{xx},\dots,u^{(n)}_{x})+u_{x}\int^{x}_{x_{0}}G(t,u,u_{z},u_{zz},\dots,u^{(m)}_{z})\,dz. (31)

The following brief notation is used for the arguments of GG: uz(k)=uz(k)​(t,z)u^{(k)}_{z}=u^{(k)}_{z}(t,z), k=0, 1,…,mk=0,\,1,\,\dots,\,m. In the special case G=s⁡(t)G=s(t) and x0=0x_{0}=0, Eq. (31) coincides with Eq. (14).

Dividing Eq. (31) by uxu_{x}, differentiating with respect to xx, and passing to the von Mises variables (8), we obtain

ηt=η2​∂∂u​(Fη)+η​G,\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\frac{F}{\eta}\right)+\eta G, (32)

where F=F⁡(t,u,η,η​ηu,η​(η​ηu)u,…)F=F(t,u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u},\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u},\dots) and G=G⁡(t,u,η,η​ηu,η​(η​ηu)u,…)G=G(t,u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u},\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u},\dots).

Equations (31) and (32) are related by the nonlocal Bäcklund transformation

ut=F⁡(t,u,η,ηx,…,ηx(n−1))+η​∫x0xG⁡(t,u,uz,uz​z,…,uz(m))​dz,ux=η.\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\displaystyle F(t,u,\eta,\eta_{x},\dots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{x})+\eta\int^{x}_{x_{0}}G(t,u,u_{z},u_{zz},\dots,u^{(m)}_{z})\,dz,\\ u_{x}&=&\eta.\end{array} (33)

Example. Let us choose the following functions in Eq. (31):

F=f1​(t,u)​ux+f2​(t,u)+f3​(t,u)​ux​xux2,G=g1​(t,u)​ux+g2​(t,u)+g3​(t,u)​ux​xux2.\begin{array}[]{rl}F&\displaystyle=f_{1}(t,u)u_{x}+f_{2}(t,u)+f_{3}(t,u)\frac{u_{xx}}{u_{x}^{2}},\\[12.0pt] G&\displaystyle=g_{1}(t,u)u_{x}+g_{2}(t,u)+g_{3}(t,u)\frac{u_{xx}}{u_{x}^{2}}.\end{array} (34)

Transformation (33)–(34) leads to the partial differential equation

ηt=η2​∂∂u​(f1+f2η+f3​ηuη2)+g1​η2+g2​η+g3​ηu.\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(f_{1}+\frac{f_{2}}{\eta}+f_{3}\frac{\eta_{u}}{\eta^{2}}\right)+g_{1}\eta^{2}+g_{2}\eta+g_{3}\eta_{u}.

With the change of variable η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta, it is reduced to the linear equation

ζt=∂∂u​(f3​ζu−f2​ζ−f1)+g3​ζu−g2​ζ−g1.\zeta_{t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\bigl(f_{3}\zeta_{u}-f_{2}\zeta-f_{1}\bigr)+g_{3}\zeta_{u}-g_{2}\zeta-g_{1}.

Remark. The integro-differential equation (31) can be reduced, by dividing by uxu_{x} and differentiating with respect to xx, to a partial differential equation containing a mixed derivative.

6 A new class of nonlinear equations with mixed
derivatives that admit order reduction

By setting G=a⁡(t)​uG=a(t)u in Eq. (31) and substituting

w⁡(t,x)=∫x0xu⁡(t,z)​𝑑z,w(t,x)=\int^{x}_{x_{0}}u(t,z)\,dz, (35)

one arrives at the following (n+1)(n+1)st-order differential equation with a mixed derivative:

wt​x=a⁡(t)​w​wx​x+F⁡(t,wx,wx​x,…,wx(n+1)).w_{tx}=a(t)ww_{xx}+F(t,w_{x},w_{xx},\dots,w^{(n+1)}_{x}). (36)

Nonlinear (n+1)(n+1)st-order equations of the form (36) can be reduced, using substitution (35) and applying the Bäcklund transformation (33) with G=a⁡(t)​u​(t,z)G=a(t)u(t,z), to the nnth-order equation

ηt=η2​∂∂u​(Fη)+a⁡(t)​u​η,F=F⁡(t,u,η,η​ηu,η​(η​ηu)u,…).\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\frac{F}{\eta}\right)+a(t)u\eta,\quad F=F(t,u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u},\eta(\eta\eta_{u})_{u},\dots).

Example 1 (generalized Calogero equation). The nonlinear second-order equation with a mixed derivative

wt​x=[f⁡(t,wx)+a⁡(t)​w]​wx​x+g⁡(t,wx)w_{tx}=[f(t,w_{x})+a(t)w]w_{xx}+g(t,w_{x}) (37)

is a special case of Eq. (36) with F=f⁡(t,wx)​wx​x+g⁡(t,wx)F=f(t,w_{x})w_{xx}+g(t,w_{x}). Substitution (35) brings Eq. (37) to an equation of the form (31):

ut=f⁡(t,u)​ux+g⁡(t,u)+a⁡(t)​ux​∫x0xu⁡(t,z)​𝑑z.u_{t}=f(t,u)u_{x}+g(t,u)+a(t)u_{x}\int^{x}_{x_{0}}u(t,z)\,dz. (38)

The nonlocal Bäcklund transformation (33) with G=a⁡(t)​u​(t,z)G=a(t)u(t,z) reduces Eq. (38) to the equation

ηt=η2​∂∂u​[f⁡(t,u)+g⁡(t,u)η]+a⁡(t)​u​η,\eta_{t}=\eta^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left[f(t,u)+\frac{g(t,u)}{\eta}\right]+a(t)u\eta,

which becomes linear after substituting η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta.

In the special case of a⁡(t)=1a(t)=1, f⁡(t,wx)=0f(t,w_{x})=0, and g⁡(t,wx)=g⁡(wx)g(t,w_{x})=g(w_{x}), Eq. (37) becomes the Calogero equation [5, 20, 21].

Example 2. Consider the nonlinear third-order equation

∂2w∂t​∂x+w​∂2w∂x2−m​(∂w∂x)2=ν​∂3w∂x3+q⁡(t)​∂w∂x+p⁡(t),\frac{\partial^{2}w}{\partial t\mkern 1.0mu\partial x}+w\frac{\partial^{2}w}{\partial x^{2}}-m\left(\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\!2}=\nu\frac{\partial^{3}w}{\partial x^{3}}+q(t)\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+p(t), (39)

which arises in hydrodynamics and derives from the Navier–Stokes equations [5, 22–24]; ww is one of the fluid velocity components and ν\nu is the kinematic viscosity. With a⁡(t)=−1a(t)=-1, F=ν​ux​x+m​u2+q⁡(t)​u+q⁡(t)F=\nu u_{xx}+mu^{2}+q(t)u+q(t), and u=wxu=w_{x}, the above transformations reduce Eq. (39) to a second-order equation representable in the form

∂η∂t+[m​u2+q⁡(t)​u+p⁡(t)]​∂η∂u=[(2​m−1)​u+q⁡(t)]​η+ν​η2​∂2η∂u2.\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}+[mu^{2}+q(t)u+p(t)]\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u}=[(2m-1)u+q(t)]\eta+\nu\eta^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\eta}{\partial u^{2}}. (40)

Note that in the degenerate case of inviscid fluid (ν=0\nu=0), the original nonlinear equation (39) reduces to a first-order linear equation, Eq. (40) with ν=0\nu=0.

7 Generalization of the von Mises transformation to the case of three independent variables

The von Mises transformation can be generalized to the cases of three or more independent variables. For example, let us consider the nnth-order equation with three independent variables

F⁡(t,x,u,uy,uy​y,…,uy(n),uy​ut​y−ut​uy​y,uy​ux​y−ux​uy​y)=0.F(t,x,u,u_{y},u_{yy},\ldots,u^{(n)}_{y},u_{y}u_{ty}-u_{t}u_{yy},u_{y}u_{xy}-u_{x}u_{yy})=0. (41)

The von Mises transformation

t,x,y,u=u⁡(t,x,y)⟹t,x,u,η=η⁡(t,x,u),whereη=∂u∂y,t,\ x,\ y,\ u=u(t,x,y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t,\ x,\ u,\ \eta=\eta(t,x,u),\ \ \hbox{where}\ \ \eta=\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}, (42)

reduces the order of Eq. (41) and brings it to the form

F⁡(t,x,u,η,η​ηu,…,ηy(n−1),η​ηt,η​ηx)=0.F(t,x,u,\eta,\eta\eta_{u},\ldots,\eta^{(n-1)}_{y},\eta\eta_{t},\eta\eta_{x})=0. (43)

where the yy-derivatives are calculated as ηy(k)=η​(ηy(k−1))u\eta^{(k)}_{y}=\eta\bigl(\eta^{(k-1)}_{y}\bigr)_{u}.

Example. Consider the Prandtl system

ut+u​ux+v​uy=ν​uy​y+f⁡(t,x),ux+vy=0.\begin{array}[]{rl}u_{t}+uu_{x}+vu_{y}&=\nu u_{yy}+f(t,x),\\ u_{x}+v_{y}&=0.\end{array} (44)

It describes a plane unsteady boundary layer with pressure gradient; uu and vv are the fluid velocity components [3–5]. Let us divide the first equation by uyu_{y}, then differentiate with respect to yy, and eliminate vyv_{y} using the second equation in (44) to obtain a nonlinear third-order equation of the form (41):

uy​ut​y−ut​uy​y+u⁡(uy​ux​y−ux​uy​y)=ν⁡(uy​uy​y​y−uy​y2)−f⁡(t,x)​uy​y.u_{y}u_{ty}-u_{t}u_{yy}+u(u_{y}u_{xy}-u_{x}u_{yy})=\nu(u_{y}u_{yyy}-u_{yy}^{2})-f(t,x)u_{yy}. (45)

Applying the von Mises transformation (42) to Eq. (45) yields the second-order equation

∂η∂t+u​∂η∂x+f⁡(t,x)​∂η∂u=ν​η2​∂2η∂u2.\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}+u\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial x}+f(t,x)\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial u}=\nu\eta^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\eta}{\partial u^{2}}. (46)

Once a solution to this equation has been found, the second velocity component vv is found immediately from the first equation of (44) without integrating.

Note that Eq. (46) can be reduced, with the change of variable η=1/ζ\eta=1/\zeta, to the nonlinear heat equation

∂ζ∂t+u​∂ζ∂x+f⁡(t,x)​∂ζ∂u=ν​∂∂u​(1ζ2​∂ζ∂u).\frac{\partial\zeta}{\partial t}+u\frac{\partial\zeta}{\partial x}+f(t,x)\frac{\partial\zeta}{\partial u}=\nu\frac{\partial}{\partial u}\left(\frac{1}{\zeta^{2}}\frac{\partial\zeta}{\partial u}\right). (47)

1∘. Consider the special case f⁡(t,x)=f⁡(t)f(t,x)=f(t). We look for exact solutions to Eq. (47) in the form

ζ=Z⁡(ξ,τ),ξ=x−u​t+∫t​f​(t)​𝑑t,τ=13​t3.\zeta=Z(\xi,\tau),\quad\xi=x-ut+\int tf(t)\,dt,\quad\tau=\frac{1}{3}t^{3}.

We arrive at the integrable equation

∂Z∂τ=ν​∂∂ξ​(1Z2​∂Z∂ξ),\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\tau}=\nu\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(\frac{1}{Z^{2}}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\xi}\right), (48)

which can be reduced to the linear heat equation [19] (see also [5]).

2∘. Consider the more general case f⁡(t,x)=f⁡(t)​x+g⁡(t)f(t,x)=f(t)x+g(t). We look for exact solutions of the special form

ζ=Z⁡(ξ,τ),ξ=φ⁡(t)​x+ψ⁡(t)​u+θ⁡(t),τ=∫ψ2​(t)​𝑑t,\zeta=Z(\xi,\tau),\quad\xi=\varphi(t)x+\psi(t)u+\theta(t),\quad\tau=\int\psi^{2}(t)\,dt,

where φ=φ⁡(t)\varphi=\varphi(t), ψ=ψ⁡(t)\psi=\psi(t), and θ=θ⁡(t)\theta=\theta(t) are determined by the linear system of ordinary differential equations

φt′+f​ψ=0,ψt′+φ=0,θt′+g​ψ=0.\varphi^{\prime}_{t}+f\psi=0,\quad\psi^{\prime}_{t}+\varphi=0,\quad\theta^{\prime}_{t}+g\psi=0.

As a result, we arrive at the integrable equation (48).

8 Conclusion

We have presented wide classes of nonlinear mathematical physics equations that admit order reduction through the use of the von Mises transformation, with the unknown function taken as the new independent variable and an appropriate partial derivative taken as the new dependent variable. RF-pairs and associated Bäcklund transformations are constructed for evolution equations of general form (special cases of which are Burgers and Korteweg–de Vries type equations as well as many other nonlinear equations of mathematical physics). The results obtained are used for order reduction and constructing exact solutions of hydrodynamics equations. A generalized Calogero equation and a number of other new integrable nonlinear equations are considered.

The von Mises and Bäcklind transformations described in the paper can be used to construct other new integrable nonlinear differential and integro-differential equations of mathematical physics.
